classes: A class is a blueprint for objects: it groups related data and the methods that act on it, and each object made from it keeps its own state.
A decorator wraps a function to add behaviour before or after it runs, without changing the function body; the wrapper receives the original function and returns a new one.
A function is a named, reusable block of code that takes inputs, does one job, and can return a result.
A list is mutable and can grow or change after creation; a tuple is fixed, so use a tuple for values that must not change.
A list keeps order and duplicates; a set keeps unique items and is built for membership checks.
A loop repeats a block of code while a condition holds or for each item in a collection; make sure the condition changes so the loop ends.
A memory leak keeps unused data reachable, so memory grows over time; find retained references and release them.
A stack removes the newest item first; a queue removes the oldest item first.
A task class can store title, status, and due date, with methods to complete, reopen, and describe the task.
A transaction groups changes so they all succeed together or roll back together, keeping data consistent.
A variable is a named place that stores a value so code can read or update it later.
An API is a defined way for programs to request work from each other: named operations, agreed inputs, and predictable responses.
An index error means the code asked for a position outside the list or string; check the length first and keep indexes from zero to length minus one.
An index is a lookup structure that helps the database find rows faster, at the cost of storage and write time.
An interface is a contract: callers rely on promised inputs and outputs without knowing internal details.
Asynchronous code starts work without blocking everything else, then handles the result when it is ready.
Binary search repeatedly checks the middle of a sorted range and discards half until the target is found or absent.

Check divisibility from 2 up to the square root of the number, return false on the first exact divisor, and test 2, 3, 4, and a large prime.
Check for an empty list before indexing or averaging, and return a clear default or error message.
Check size, type, extension, and content; store uploads outside executable paths and scan when required.
Check the loop condition and the update step: the variable the condition reads must move toward the exit value on every pass, and add a safety break while debugging.
Check type, length, range, and allowed characters; reject invalid input with a clear message before using it.
Code review checks correctness, clarity, tests, security, and maintainability before changes merge.
Compare neighboring values or use a known sorting method, then verify sorted, reversed, and duplicate inputs.
Compare the string with its reverse: text == text[::-1]. Test an empty string, a single character, and a mixed-case word after normalising case.
Count requests per key in a time window, allow bursts within limits, and return clear retry guidance.
Decide where null is allowed, check before use, and prefer explicit defaults or errors over silent failure.

Define a small function with two numeric inputs, return their sum, and test it with positive, negative, and zero values.
Define required fields, types, ranges, and cross-field rules; report every validation problem clearly.
Define states, allowed transitions, events, and guards; reject transitions that are not listed.
Define the route, inputs, validation, success response, error responses, and tests for each case.

Event driven design reacts to named events, keeping producers and consumers loosely coupled.
Extract the repeated logic into one helper, keep behavior unchanged, and run the existing tests after each small change.
Feature flags switch behavior at runtime so teams can release gradually and disable risky paths quickly.
Immutable values do not change after creation, which reduces surprise side effects and simplifies reasoning.
Iterate over the collection in order and handle one item per pass; avoid changing the collection while looping.
Log important events with context, avoid secrets, use levels consistently, and make failures searchable.
Multiply the integers from 1 up to n, return 1 for 0, reject negative inputs, and test 0, 1, and 5.
Object oriented programming groups data and behavior into objects with clear responsibilities and interfaces.
Open the file safely, handle missing or unreadable files, and close resources even when an error occurs.
Open the file with a with block so it closes automatically: with open(path) as handle: text = handle.read(). Handle a missing file with a clear error.
Parse arguments, validate them, run one clear action, print helpful output, and return a proper exit code.
Password storage should use a slow salted hash designed for passwords, never a fast general hash or plain text.
Profile first, find the hot path, reduce repeated work, choose better data structures, and measure again.
Read settings from a file or environment, validate required keys, apply defaults, and fail with clear messages.
Read the error line first, check brackets, quotes, and indentation around it, fix one issue, then run again; the reported line is often just after the real mistake.
Recursion solves a problem by calling the same function on a smaller input until a base case stops the calls.
Reproduce the failure, read the first error, isolate the smallest failing case, fix one cause, then rerun the test.
Retry only temporary failures, wait longer between attempts, cap total attempts, and log the final error.
Return early when input is invalid so the main path stays flat and readable.
Return page items, total count, page size, current page, and links or cursors for the next page.
Return service status, version, and dependency checks quickly, without exposing secrets or heavy work.
Split each non-empty line on the first separator, trim spaces, validate keys, and report malformed lines.
Split text into words, normalize case if needed, count each word, and test punctuation and empty text.
Store each value with an expiry time, return fresh values quickly, and refresh or remove stale entries.

Test just below, exactly at, and just above each boundary so off-by-one errors are caught.

Trace the inputs through each line, compare the actual output with the expected one, and check operators, order of operations, and off-by-one bounds first.
Track seen values in a set and collect values that appear again, preserving first duplicate order if needed.
Trim whitespace, collapse repeated spaces, normalize case when appropriate, and test punctuation handling.

Use names that state purpose, keep functions small, and remove comments that merely repeat the code.
